intro_en:
The Israel National Trail passes along the foot of the Negev Highlands and the western edge of the Arava, through a landscape of wide open spaces and low hills. The trail is gentle and comfortable, and the walking is on wide dirt roads with no steep ascents or descents. In the middle of the segment we pass through an ancient way station, Moa, and cross the "Incense Route".

 Gav Holit – Sapir (45)
 Tzukim – Nahal Barak (47)
transport_en: At the starting point: in the community of Sapir or on the Arava Road at the turn-off to Sapir. At the end point: in the community of Tzukim or on the Arava Road at the turn-off to Tzukim
pois_en: The founding site of Ir Ovot. Moshav Tzofar. Moa.
important_en: Water can be filled at the Tzofar cemetery, close to the trail.
In Tzukim there are options for stocking up on water and food.
description_en:
From the community of Sapir we reconnect with the route of the Israel National Trail, which passes west of the community. From the main gate of the community, at the entrance from Road 90, we set out on a blue-marked road that circles the community outside the fence, heading south. Where the road turns right beside the corner of the community's fence, we turn left onto a dirt road that leads within a few minutes' walk to the junction with the route of the Israel National Trail.
The Israel National Trail follows red marking for the entire length of the segment, and begins with a climb along a dirt road to a saddle, beyond which the road and the trail continue south.
The walk runs along the foot of the Negev Highlands at the edge of the Arava, which spreads out east of the road and is characterised by a landscape of flat expanses. East of the Arava, the Edom Mountains in the Kingdom of Jordan can be seen in the distance.
The boundary line between the mountains and the plain, along which the Israel National Trail runs, is also the line of the geological fault, the Syrian-African Rift, which created the rift valley on Israel's eastern side, from the Hula Valley to the head of the Gulf of Eilat, of which the Arava is a part. Along the fault line there is water deep in the ground, and at several points north of the Sapir centre it emerges at the surface in the form of springs (Ein Rahel, Ein Shahak, Ein Tamid).
In the area there are boreholes and wells for pumping water for the use of the Arava communities. Alongside the road and the trail runs a pipe carrying water pumped from boreholes; it is buried in the ground and marked with iron posts. Above ground we can see the line's service installations: fenced-off pipes and valves.
The Israel National Trail runs parallel to the boundary of a large nature reserve, the Tzinim Cliff (Matzok HaTzinim) Nature Reserve. The reserve's territory stretches from Sde Boker to Tzofar. On the right we see from time to time brown metal posts marking the boundary of the reserve. Rest breaks can be taken in the shade of the acacia trees scattered over the area, outside the reserve.
After about an hour's walk, the road climbs onto a low ridge. After a further short distance, to the right of the road and at the foot of a hill, we see the remains of a structure built of local stone. Here the small community of Ir Ovot began its life in 1967. Simcha Perlmutter, an American Jew, led a group of young people who established a settlement in the Arava and named it after one of the stations of the Children of Israel on their journey from Egypt through the desert. According to the story, the settlement's first location was decided by the driver of the truck carrying the equipment on the day the group arrived in the Arava. When they reached the area the driver declared, "I'm not driving any further," and threw the equipment off the truck. In the early days of Ir Ovot, its residents made their living from a kiosk they set up beside the Arava Road, which they called Sukkat Ovot. Later Perlmutter and his people moved to Ein Hatzeva, at the foot of the historic tell. The settlement has since gone through several incarnations, and today only a handful of families live there; in recent years a plan was published to build a large community for hundreds of families at the site.
To the east lies Moshav Tzofar, established in 1968 as a Nahal outpost settlement; before it, the moshavim Ein Yahav and Hatzeva were established in the central Arava. Later the moshavim Paran and Idan were built in the area. Agriculture is the main source of livelihood for the Arava moshavim, and thanks to the great heat, vegetables ripen earlier than in other regions, which allows vegetables and fruit to be marketed in the winter months. In addition, thanks to the dryness and the isolation from the agricultural areas of central Israel, the Arava is relatively free of pests and diseases. In aerial photographs of the area, the green patches added by the agricultural land along the central Arava, from Idan in the north to Paran in the south, stand out clearly, as the prophet said: "The wilderness and the parched land shall be glad; and the desert (Arava) shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose" (Isaiah 35).
About a kilometre east of the trail is the Antelope Farm, where water can be filled. The Israel National Trail advances past Ir Ovot and passes a chicken-coop farm whose roofs have been fitted with solar panels for generating electricity. At the corner of the farm the trail turns left and passes between the coop farm and a reservoir. We circle the reservoir to its southern corner, and from there the trail continues south; after a short walk we cross a dirt road. On the left, north of the road, there is a Mekorot facility for diluting water pumped from local wells with a high salinity level. Beside the facility grow Washingtonia palm trees, surrounded by a green patch of vegetation that benefits from water overflowing from the facility.
Please note: the trail passes close to the cemetery of Moshav Tzofar, a possible water-filling point.
After a few minutes' walk we reach a road junction: a black-marked road turns left towards the Arava Road (90). The Israel National Trail, alongside the red marking, continues south from here. To the right of the junction we see a hill with a short trail climbing to it: this is Horvat Moa.
Moa is an ancient way station established on the trade route of the Incense Route, which ran between the Arabian Peninsula and the shores of the Mediterranean and flourished especially in the Nabataean period. Along the route of the ancient road, way stations were built to serve the camel caravans crossing the desert, carrying goods, mainly perfumes and spices. The Israel National Trail passes close to two more similar stations: Metzad Mahmal and Metzad Saharonim in Makhtesh Ramon.
It is recommended to go into the site and take in the structures and finds. At the site we can see a fortress and a caravanserai (khan), bathhouses, an olive press and a complex water system. In the archaeological excavation carried out at Moa between 1981 and 1984, pottery vessels, coins of Roman emperors, mats, textiles, wooden vessels, olive and date stones, and nut and almond shells were also found. The excavation showed that Moa was established in the second and third centuries BCE and operated until the end of the third century CE.
From Moa, the Israel National Trail advances west to a trail junction where the Israel National Trail turns south, together with the red marking. The road that continues straight on is marked black and climbs west into the Negev towards Nahal Nekarot and Makhtesh Ramon, along the ancient route of the Incense Route.
We walk about 4 km through Arava scenery with low hills and acacias scattered in the gullies. Along the way we can practise identifying the species of the acacia trees. A simple but not certain way to distinguish between the two species common in the area, the twisted acacia (Acacia raddiana) and the umbrella thorn acacia (Acacia tortilis), is by the shape of the tree's canopy. The twisted acacia usually has a single trunk that branches out. The umbrella thorn acacia usually has several trunks emerging from ground level, and the tree's canopy is shaped like a canopy, a flat umbrella. A more precise identification can be made from the leaves and fruits. In the umbrella thorn acacia the leaves and fruits are small and hairy, while in the twisted acacia the leaves are almost entirely hairless and the fruits are large and completely bald. The umbrella thorn acacia is more drought-resistant and heat-loving, and it manages even in relatively small gullies.
On the stretch before the meeting with Nahal Ashosh, the terrain is bare and almost treeless. The appearance of the first acacia trees signals that we are nearing the trail junction where we turn off to the community of Tzukim. Two large acacia trees pressed against the wall on the left side of the gully announce that we have reached the turn.
Here we leave the Israel National Trail and turn left with green marking onto a road that heads east in the channel of Nahal Ashosh, towards the Arava Road and the community of Tzukim.
On the way to Tzukim, we descend along a stream channel. At first it narrows and the distance between the rock walls on either side closes in, and further on the channel widens again. After walking about 4 km we reach the Arava Road. From here we can walk south alongside the road for about 700 metres to the entrance to the community of Tzukim, where we can stock up on water and food.
Tzukim, built on the southern bank of Nahal Ashosh, is the youngest of the communities of the central Arava. It was established in 2004 as an initiative of a group of people from central Israel who sought to found a community in the Arava focused mainly on tourism.
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, Trail Marking Coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel.
